question: Over the next five days, I am going to use ChatGPT to recreate iconic album covers. Will they be recognizable?
description:
The process works like this:

Step 1: feed ChatGPT an album cover and ask it to describe it

[image]Step 2: take its response and remove mentions of the album name

[image]Step 3: start a new chat and ask it to generate its own image description

[image]Step 4: I post the results to Manifold, asking, "Which album is ChatGPT recreating with this image?" I will make it a multiple choice market which allows people to add answers. The answer I add will always be Trout Mask Replica, and it will never be correct. Each market will stay open for two weeks.

[image]Resolution: I will be doing this once a day for the next five days. I will consider each image to "be recognizable" if the highest probability answer for a given market is correct. So, if in the Abbey Road market, the Abbey Road choice had the highest probability, I would consider Manifold to have recognized it.

For this market to resolve as yes, I will need three or more of the five markets to converge on the correct answer. Otherwise, it resolves as no.

Considering I've already used the most famous album art of all time, the examples I use will be more difficult. I have no perfect way of quantifying what makes an album "iconic", but I will do my best to choose albums that music nerds are largely aware of. I will at least promise to only include albums with at least one song that has more than ten million streams on Spotify.

I will be taking the first response from the AI for both the image description and generation in order to avoid cherry-picking.

question: Will I earn at least $25 per hour grading USA(J)MO?
description:
I am a grader for USA(J)MO. Let M be the amount of money that I earn from this (pre-tax). I will estimate the hours spent H as follows:

For each problem P I grade, using a period of uninterrupted grading near the middle of my grading experience for that problem, I will estimate R_P, the amount of papers that I grade per hour in an ideal setting. These will be rounded to the nearest tenth.

I will sum the amount of papers I graded divided by R_P over all problems P.

The reason that I am using this procedure is that I often grade in non-ideal conditions (e.g. while eating, while in class, etc.) which decrease the amount of papers I grade per hour, and it would be unfair to weight this time equally.

Finally, I will add 1/6 hour (10 minutes) per conflict that I am involved in and that I take nonzero effort in resolving. (These occur when I assign a different score from another grader, and we need to agree on a score.)

This market resolves YES if M >= 25*H. Otherwise, it resolves NO.

After USA(J)MO scores are released, I will release the the set of all problems I graded, and for each problem the value R_P, the amount of papers I graded, and the number of conflicts I had. This will be when H will be computed. M will be computed (and the market resolved) at the time that MAA pays me or EOY 2026, whichever occurs first.

Disclaimer: The monetary payment had little impact on my decision to be a grader, and has little impact on how much I decide to grade.

question: Is RLHF good for AI safety? [resolves to poll]
description:
Resolution Criteria

Resolves to the majority result of a YES/NO poll of Manifold users at the end of 2025 for the question, "Is RLHF good for AI safety?"

Explanation of RLHF and AI Safety

One of the most common approaches to AI safety right now is reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), in which the AI system such as GPT-4 is trained to maximize a reward signal from human feedback. For example, if the AI is asked, "Should I help or hurt people?" human feedback would presumably favor the response, "Yes," or, "Yes, you shouldn't hurt people." RLHF seems like a tractable way to make AI systems more useful and beneficial, at least in the short run, and it has arguably been one of the biggest advances in large language model (LLM) capabilities since 2020. Unlike many AI safety approaches, RLHF has tangible benefits today that could make it easier to iterate and improve upon and to popularize it before we build artificial general intelligence (AGI) .

On the other hand, RLHF could be bad in the long run. It could lead to AIs that seem aligned, helpful, honest, and harmless because they say nice-sounding things but are actually misalinged. In other words, it may be optimizing for seeming aligned and not for being aligned, which may be very different. People might not worry as much about misalignment if they see RLHF systems as opposed to non-RLHF systems. Moreover, because RLHF makes LLMs so much more useful, it seems to speed up timelines to AGI and gives humanity less time to work on AI safety prior to an intelligence explosion. Overall, this could increase the likelihood of deception, a "sharp left turn," and existential catastrophe. Of course there are many more plausible arguments on the topic, such as that maybe we should speed towards AGI so we build it before humanity has even more computational power (e.g., Moore's Law).

More technical detail on RLHF is available in Ouyang et al. (2022). A more accessible video explanation is availabe from HuggingFace on YouTube.
creator: Ace
